claims.text: Electrochemical dealloying can produce a three-dimensional nanoframework from a noble-metal-based high-entropy alloy precursor.
The resulting nanoframework will be stable.
The resulting nanoframework will have high surface area.
The precursor may be a solution-cast or homogenized ingot containing both noble and less noble elements.
Applying a controlled electrochemical potential in an appropriate electrolyte will preferentially dissolve the less noble elements.
The applied potential should exceed the dissolution threshold of the less noble species.
The dealloying conditions should preserve or passivate the noble components.
Selective removal of lower-standard-potential elements leaves a porous, noble-metal-rich framework.
Differences in electrochemical potentials cause less noble species to dissolve preferentially.
Preferential dissolution produces interconnected pores within the residual noble-metal network.
The residual noble-metal network is resistant to dissolution.
The three-dimensional nanoframework will improve catalytic accessibility.
Electrochemical dealloying will provide enhanced control over pore morphology and composition.
Conventional processing of noble-metal-based high-entropy alloys commonly yields solid, less porous structures lacking extended surface area.
Successful dealloying is limited by the magnitude of the differences in element reduction potentials.
Potential and electrolyte tuning are required to avoid over-dissolution or problematic passivation.
Failure to observe a continuous three-dimensional porous network would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to observe selective dissolution of less noble elements would falsify the hypothesis.
